On the night of Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Udayaditya disarmed and bound Sitaram at the guard’s request, allowing the prince to pass while protecting Sitaram from punishment. Sitaram refused to fight Udayaditya because the prince had twice saved his life. Later, their roles reversed: Sitaram opened Udayaditya’s prison door during the fire, carried him out and guided the helpless prince toward escape.

Pratapaditya first sends two Pathan brothers to kill Basanta Ray on his way to Jessore. One lures away his retainers, but the other befriends Basanta Ray and confesses the plot instead of killing him.

Later, Pratapaditya orders Basanta Ray’s execution at Raigarh. Muktiyar Khan and his soldiers enter the fort in disguise, and a soldier named Abdul kills the old king with a sword.

In Jessore’s inner quarters, Ramai was disguised as a middle-aged woman; Rammohan seized and carried him out. In the king’s room in Chandradwip, Ramai wore no stated disguise; Rammohan threw him out after he mocked Vibha, who had been mistaken for a beggar.
Mangala secretly prepared poison for Surma, causing her death before she could leave for her father’s house.

Her husband, Ramchandra Ray, takes her refusal as an insult and decides to marry another woman. By the time Vibha reaches Chandradwip, she has lost her place in his palace and her hopes of happiness are shattered.

Rukmini obtained Udayaditya’s ring after demanding it from him. Sitaram and Bhagavat then used its engraved seal to stamp a forged petition claiming that Udayaditya had accused Pratapaditya of treason to gain the kingdom. Bhagavat gave the petition to Pratapaditya, falsely claiming he had intercepted it on its way to the Emperor. Pratapaditya ordered Udayaditya imprisoned, though he admitted he did not particularly believe the accusation.

Udayaditya helped Ramchandra escape by overpowering the guards, after which Pratapaditya dismissed them. Feeling responsible for their hardship, Udayaditya gave them stipends, angering Pratapaditya, who forbade further help. Surma then secretly arranged payments to their families. When Pratapaditya learned of this defiance, he ordered her sent to her paternal home.

The song expresses Basanta Ray’s loneliness and grief for loved ones who are gone and the happiness they once shared. He first sings it alone at sunset in Raigarh, longing for those he used to visit and sing for. Later, in Jessore, he sings it while holding Vibha’s hand after seeing Surma’s empty room and the remnants of a once-happy family.

After failing to stop the escape, Rukmini told Pratapaditya that Basanta Ray and Sitaram had helped Udayaditya flee. She led men to Raigarh, where they confirmed Udayaditya’s whereabouts. Pratapaditya then sent Muktiyar Khan to capture Udayaditya and execute Basanta Ray. Rukmini helped the soldiers find Udayaditya, and Muktiyar’s soldier Abdul killed Basanta Ray.

Pratapaditya received Ramchandra coolly, giving him little attention and making him feel inferior. Later, Ramchandra allowed his courtiers to ridicule Pratapaditya as his social inferior, and took pleasure in their insults.

Rukmini leaves Raigarh, changes her name to Mangala, and settles near Jessore, hoping to win Udayaditya and rule alongside him. She befriends palace servants and learns of the royal family’s hostility toward his wife, Surma. When the queen sends for a remedy to draw Udayaditya away from Surma, Rukmini prepares poison. Surma dies, though the palace believes she took poison herself.

Later, Rukmini enters Udayaditya’s bedchamber and pleads for his love, claiming he ruined her. He refuses her advances and gives her a ring to make her leave, then grieves for Surma.

Udayaditya initially wishes he had not been born crown prince, feeling unfit to rule and burdened by his father’s scrutiny and neglect. Later, blaming his own weakness for the ruin of those who loved him, he asks Pratapaditya to release him from the throne. Before his father, he swears at Ma-Kali’s feet never to claim any of Jessore’s kingdom, sit on its throne, or touch its scepter. He names Samaraditya as heir and prepares to leave for Kashi.

Ramchandra wrote to Pratapaditya declaring that he had renounced Vibha and that she should not be sent to Chandradwip. Rammohan refused to carry the letter, so Ramchandra sent Nayanchand, who feared Pratapaditya’s reaction and gave it to the Mahishi instead.

The Mahishi hid the letter from Vibha and Pratapaditya and showed it to Basanta Ray. Believing Ramchandra had written in anger and would relent if Vibha returned, Basanta advised the Mahishi to announce that he had requested Vibha’s return. She told Vibha and the household this, leaving Vibha overjoyed and convinced of her husband’s love.

Pratapaditya had the palace canal blocked with sal logs and ordered the inner quarters sealed. But Udayaditya opened the guarded doors, and Rammohan lowered Ramchandra from the palace roof into his boat using a rope made of sheets. Rammohan and his men then pulled the boat over the logs. The guards’ stones fell short, they could not promptly ready a gun, and their pursuit boat arrived too late. Ramchandra escaped into the Bhairav river.

The sitar was Basanta Ray’s constant companion, but when he was forced to leave Udayaditya, his grief made him unable to play it, and he left it behind, saying he would never play again. Later, he says its strings are broken and it can no longer be tuned, reflecting the loss of joy and companionship he feels in their separation. The news of Udayaditya’s imprisonment deepens that despair.

Earlier, Udayaditya would fight oppression and protect subjects without considering the consequences. After Surma’s death, a paralysing fear of Pratapaditya makes him hesitate and withdraw: he abandons an attempt to prevent a raid, flees rather than stop a subject’s beating, and fails to send money to those in need.
Sitaram helps Udayaditya escape from the prison where he was confined because of the forged petition. During a fire, he opens the prison door and leads him out.

- To rescue Ramchandra Ray, Rammohan ties sheets into a rope, carries him down from the palace roof on his back, then grips the rope with his teeth so he can lower him safely into a boat. He then helps pull the boat over logs blocking the canal.
- When Vibha faints after Ramchandra rejects her, Rammohan lifts her, carries her out of the palace, places her in a palanquin, and returns to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is elaborately dressed by her mother in thick gold bangles, diamond bracelets, a large nose ring, and an elaborate coiffure. Though burdened by the finery, she is shy and radiant with joy at Ramchandra’s arrival.

In Chandradwip, after learning he is marrying someone else, she rejects a palanquin and goes on foot dressed as a common woman, saying she will approach him like a beggar. She enters the palace without a welcome and falls tearfully at his feet; he mistakes her for a beggar seeking alms.

In his bedchamber, the window is a place of grief and remembrance, where Udayaditya leaves Surma’s place empty and hopes to see her again. In prison, the small window becomes a source of hope and freedom: the sky and birds remind him that no ruler can imprison him forever.

Sitaram, attracted to both Rukmini’s beauty and her money, borrows from her amid flirtatious banter and never repays her. They later confer secretly, but their relationship turns hostile when Udayaditya is imprisoned: Sitaram blames Rukmini, threatens to ruin and humiliate her, and vows to free the prince. Rukmini, possessive of Udayaditya herself, vows to stop him.

After helping Udayaditya escape, Sitaram visits Rukmini’s cottage intending to steal her money, believing her dead. He finds her alive and enraged. She threatens to kill both him and Udayaditya, and his attempt to charm her only makes her angrier. When she goes for a curved blade, he flees; she returns and strikes the floor where he stood. Outside, Sitaram worries she will expose the escape and regrets not strangling her.

Sitaram and his allies set the guards’ huts on fire, drawing the guards away and creating chaos while he led Udayaditya out of prison and to a boat. His men prolonged the distraction by sabotaging the firefighting.

After Udayaditya escaped, they set his empty cell ablaze. Sitaram threw bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword into it, while false reports of screams and a collapsed roof helped spread the story that he had died in the fire. Sitaram also intercepted the letters Udayaditya had sent to the palace and destroyed one. The deception briefly worked, but Rukmini exposed the escape, and later sightings confirmed it.

Ramchandra Ray assumes Udayaditya saved him mainly for Vibha’s sake, not out of concern for him. Taking the rescue for granted, he feels no gratitude and joins his courtiers in mocking Udayaditya for being Pratapaditya’s son.

Pratapaditya dismissed warnings about the Emperor’s anger, even after hearing that a complaint had been lodged against him. Later, Bhagavat and Sitaram forged a petition accusing Pratapaditya of treason, using Udayaditya’s seal to make it appear that the prince had appealed to the Emperor to gain the kingdom. Bhagavat brought it to Pratapaditya, claiming he had intercepted it on its way to Delhi. The context describes the king’s reaction but does not explicitly describe Udayaditya’s imprisonment.

When Surma is present, Vibha turns to her to have her hair styled as she likes, a small act of affection and understanding in contrast to her mother’s controlling adornment. After Surma is gone, Vibha waits in vain for her to braid it, and her hair remains unbraided. Later, its unkempt state visibly reflects Vibha’s grief, loneliness, and loss of Surma’s care.
